title: What is an interview rubric? Build and use guide
summary: Build an interview rubric that panels adopt: define competencies, set calibrated scales and weights, and score candidates on evidence rather than instinct.
body_text: Most interviewers can intuitively grasp the purpose of an interview rubric. The problem is building one your interview panels want to use. To encourage adoption, you need a resource that’s easy for interviewers to implement and makes their jobs easier. In this guide, we’ll walk you through how to build functional interview rubrics that help hiring managers evaluate candidates objectively. Along the way, we’ll define how these rubrics work and what to include to keep scoring consistent. What is an interview rubric? Interview rubrics are structured guides used by interviewers to evaluate different candidates for a role against the same set of job-relevant criteria. A complete rubric has three parts: Competencies: Rubrics detail the skills and ideal behaviors a role requires. They should also provide short definitions for each competency to leave no room for ambiguity. Rating scale: Rubrics include a fixed scale, such as 1–4 or 1–5, where each number on the scale represents a pre-defined meaning. Example benchmarks: Rubrics also include behavioral indicators, short descriptors of what a 2, for example, sounds like when compared to other numbers on the scale. This makes it easier for interviewers to tie what candidates say or demonstrate to a specific score, instead of going off of gut feeling. Interview rubrics vs interview scorecards: What is the difference? While the two terms are often used interchangeably, interview rubrics and scorecards refer to different artifacts in practice. Rubrics are the standard-bearing frameworks for a role. Your team builds them once per role to define competencies, the ratings scale, and example benchmarks. Interview scorecards, on the other hand, are the live documents filled out during the interview to record candidate answers and provide a score. Take the example of an open role with a four-person hiring panel interviewing six candidates. The hiring team creates the rubric first, one time. Then the individual interviewers use the rubric to create 24 different interview scorecards, one for each interview. Why interview rubrics improve hiring Rubrics ensure that candidate-specific evidence is used to drive interviewer recommendations and that the defined job criteria are applied consistently. Some tangible ways rubrics improve hiring include: Quality of hire: Scoring based on pre-defined competencies helps ensure candidates are advanced based on the demonstrative behaviors that predict success in a role, rather than factors like general likeability, pedigree, or a vague sense of cultural fit. Speed and alignment: When panels assess candidates on the same scale, disagreements that arise in the debrief are easier to reconcile, allowing teams to forge alignment and move forward faster. Fairness and compliance: Hiring decisions can be challenged in the future. But using a rubric with defined competencies and scales creates a paper trail that helps panels defend decisions if needed. Candidate experience: Every candidate gets asked the same questions and is held to the same standard, making it easier for interviewers to provide concrete feedback when asked. Common reasons rubrics fail Rubrics don’t usually fail because of some inherent flaw in the competencies selected by hiring panels or the framework they use to score candidates. They fail because rubrics fossilize into untouched documents that never make it into the interview or influence proceedings. Some other common failure points: Vague scales: A scale labeled 1–5 without concrete definitions and examples of behavior or competencies at each step sets up your interviewers to rely on instinct instead of evidence. And relying on instinct can lead to unconscious biases that unfairly skew the hiring process. Misweighted priorities: If the nice-to-have skills carry the same weight as core job requirements, the rubric doesn’t accurately reflect the bar for candidates to clear. Delayed scoring: When interviewers wait until too long after the interview to record scores, solid evidence tends to be replaced by vague impressions. Opinion-based notes: Comments with no evidence behind them ("strong communicator") leave nothing to compare against, so the bar shifts from candidate to candidate depending on who's assessing. What to include in a rubric Rubrics get adopted when they’re specific to roles and encourage interviewers to rely on evidence. Two core sets of elements come together to make that happen. Competencies and question alignment Start by defining core competencies drawn from the job’s requirements, not a template. Finding the right balance is key; include too few competencies, and interviewers will feel it’s missing important context. Too many, and you risk interviewers glossing over them. Each competency should include a short definition and be mapped to specific questions (and vice versa). Build competencies without questions, and you risk interviewers inventing their own inconsistent questions. Build questions without attached competencies, and interviewers end up with potentially helpful information, but no way to map it to the core job requirements in the hiring process. Scoring and evidence fields On the scoring side, rubrics should include the following: Calibrated rating scales: Where each point maps to a written definition. Behavioral indicators: Each point in a score should describe what an answer at that level conveys. Weights: Core competencies that drive success in the role should be properly weighted. Comment fields: For interviewers to easily and consistently record their remarks in one place. Overall scoring ranges: Tie these to a decision, so scores map cleanly to “advance,” “hold,” or “reject” recommendations. How to build and use interview rubrics Building and using your interview rubric is a continuous workflow that extends from role calibration all the way to post-interview review. Here’s how to run it. Build the rubric around competencies and questions Hold a calibration conversation with the hiring manager before you put the first candidate interview on your calendar. Then, ask what success looks like for this new hire in their first six months on the job. That answer informs the core competencies you’ll be hiring for. From there: Define role-specific competencies: In one sentence, if possible, in terms everyone on the interview panel understands. Define score meanings: Articulate what makes a 2 a 2 and a 4 a 4, then fill in the rest of the steps between them on the ratings scale. Assign weights: Work backward from the most essential competencies, making sure core skills and behaviors are highlighted. Write standardized questions: Ensure these are tied to job outcomes, with examples of follow-up prompts in case interviewers need to drill down for evidence. Add a notes field: These should live under each competency and be required for each interviewer to fill out. Use the rubric during and after interviews During the interview, lean on the assessment questions defined in the rubric and use the notes field to actively jot down evidence. Try to capture what candidates say, including verbatim quotes where possible. Then, review the evidence to score the candidate for each competency as soon as the interview ends. The longer you wait to finish scoring, the fuzzier your memory gets, so it’s best to finalize ratings as soon as possible. The evidence that matters most varies depending on the type of role you’re hiring. In an SDR interview, for example, it’s not enough to hear that the candidate is resilient; try to get them to explain in detail how they handle rejection and what they’ve changed specifically in the past when working through a rough sales stretch. For software engineer interviews, on the other hand, you want to understand how candidates approach technical problems—e.g., whether they can articulate any trade-offs between different approaches—not just hear an answer devoid of context. These sorts of deep candidate insights are exactly what rubrics are for and where they prove their value in the evaluation process. Next steps for consistent scoring Teams unlock consistent scoring when they use rubrics to recalibrate their hiring, not just evaluate candidates. The scores a panel produces—and how effectively they achieve alignment—are themselves records of how well a particular rubric performs. As roles, candidate expectations, and markets evolve, reviewing rubrics becomes necessary to ensure they don’t drift from their intended purpose. Calibration and drift review Teams should aim to review rubric data on a quarterly basis, or after a set number of interviews (10–15) for high-volume roles. Three patterns worth keeping an eye out for: Consistently low-scoring competencies: If most or all candidates are routinely earning low marks on a specific competency, odds are good that something is misaligned. Questions might be framed incorrectly, or the bar might be set too high for the role's expected seniority level. Interviewer leniency: If one interviewer on the panel’s candidates are averaging a full point higher than the others’ for their assigned competency, they might be waving candidates along without the proper scrutiny. Score drift across panels: On some panels, scores tend to drift upwards over time when interviewers start comparing candidates against each other, and not the rubric itself. In any of the above scenarios, taking the time to recalibrate with the panel members or retool problem areas in the rubric itself is a valuable intervention that drives improved consistency over time. Operationalizing the rubric Remember: Rubrics earn staying power when they live in the systems your team already uses. Get a few key elements right, and adopting the rubric becomes the path of least resistance. One of these is using embedded score capture in the tools your team already has open. This ensures scorecards get filled out inside the interview window, and not hours (or days) later once recall has already been significantly degraded. Keep one standard-bearing rubric per role. Copying the rubric into a new document for each search allows small tweaks to accumulate over time; eventually, your interviewers are unwittingly working with completely different documents. Filtering reports by competency and user makes those changes visible. Finally, connecting the entire workflow to your ATS keeps scoring history attached to the role, and not stowed away in various team members’ folders. Start with a stronger candidate pool A scoring framework makes your evaluations consistent, but it can only sort the candidates who reach the interview. If the shortlist is thin, better scoring just gives you a clearer view of the same limited options. Let Juicebox handle the sourcing. Describe the role in plain language and Juicebox searches across a large candidate pool to surface best-fit candidates, including the people who aren't applying, so your rubric has stronger candidates to work with. Frequently asked questions What are interview rubrics? Interview rubrics are structured scoring guides used to evaluate candidates against the same set of job-relevant criteria. Rubrics define competencies, assign a rating scale and weights, and provide behavioral indicators describing the type of evidence from candidates that justify a given score. What is a rubric for interviews? A rubric for interviews is the framework a hiring team uses to score candidates. It’s built once per role and used for every candidate in that search. What is an example of an interview rubric? An example rubric for an SDR might measure four competencies: e.g., prospecting approach, objection handling, resilience, and coachability. Each competency will carry a percentage weight that aligns with its importance relative to the others; prospecting might account for 30% of the total, while a lesser factor like coachability would count for 20%. Each competency is anchored by behavioral indicators that help interviewers discern a candidate's score on a set scale, such as 1–4. Lower scores might indicate the candidate answers the question without providing specifics, while higher scores involve a thorough description of the candidate’s experience and aptitude with concrete examples.

title: Innovation at AES
summary: AES' innovations drive the clean energy transition with pioneering solar, energy storage, and AI solutions.
body_text: Innovation at AES AES Next AES Next builds and invests in a portfolio of high-growth businesses and strategic partnerships that drive the global energy transition. By identifying key challenges and opportunities in the energy sector, we apply deep industry expertise to develop and scale breakthrough solutions—from pioneering energy storage to revolutionizing solar deployment—creating tangible value for our company, partners, and communities. AES Next Portfolio AES Next follows a proven approach to identity, select, develop and scale strategic business opportunities to create long-term value for our business, our partners and the industry. Maximo: revolutionizing solar installation through robotics To keep up with increased energy demand, AES developed Maximo, the first AI-enabled solar robot for the end-to-end installation of solar modules. Skilled construction crews rely on Maximo to improve speed and safety by automating the strenuous heavy lifting of solar panels to accelerate solar installation. Meet Maximo Safer Maximo automates the heavy lifting of solar plans, reducing strenuous work and lifting by 90%. Faster Maximo makes solar deployment 2x faster than traditional methods and accelerates the delivery of more megawatts in less time, utilizing a mobile microgrid and AI-enabled computer vision for precise module placement. Cost Effective Maximo reduces time to power, enhances safety and accessibility, and enables EPCs and solar project developers to deliver more solar cost-effectively and efficiently than traditional installation methods. AI Fund: Co-building AI-powered startups Through our partnership with Andrew Ng's AI Fund, we’re co-building AI-powered startups that accelerate the energy transition. By incubating and investing in cutting-edge AI solutions, we’re not just adapting to the future of energy; we’re creating it. Meet AI Fund Context & insight The industry urgently needs solutions that optimize energy generation and storage management, enhance worksite safety, and expand access to clean energy finance. By combining AES’s energy expertise with AI Fund’s leadership in AI, we’re tackling some of the industry’s most pressing challenges faster and smarter than ever before. Action AES and AI Fund developed a fast-track incubation model to identify, fund, and launch AI-powered energy solutions. This agile, venture-driven approach ensures that the most impactful ideas get scaled quickly, delivering next-level results for customers and the energy sector. Outcome 3 companies co-founded in the first year of partnership In just six months, our first startup progressed from concept to funding Fluence: scaling energy storage Building on our pioneering work in lithium-ion storage, AES joined forces with Siemens to launch Fluence, a global leader in grid-scale energy storage, supercharging the energy transition with award-winning technology and AI-optimized solutions. Meet Fluence Context & insight Energy storage was viewed as risky, unknown technology when we first started pioneering the technology. We knew it had untapped potential that was key to unlocking a more sustainable and reliable energy future. Action AES was the first to go big into utility-scale batteries in 2007 and built one of the world’s largest battery fleets over the next decade. Siemens is one of the world’s biggest energy and grid technology providers. We joined together in 2017 to create the industry powerhouse Fluence, dedicated to innovating modern electric infrastructure. Outcome Today, Fluence is a global leader in energy storage and digital optimization. We are accelerating the energy transition with gigawatts of projects successfully contracted, deployed, and under management across nearly 50 markets worldwide.

title: Form with conditionals vs. multiple forms in the same card: which organization should you choose?
summary: See when to use a form with conditionals and when to use multiple forms in the same open card in Jestor.
body_text: In Jestor , an open card can either have a single form with conditional fields that appear or disappear based on set rules, or several independent forms in different side panels, each with its own purpose. When an overly long form gets in the way More complex processes — like multi-step approvals or record-heavy intake forms — suffer when everything sits in a single long form, even if it's well organized with conditionals. That forces the user to scroll through the entire screen to find the right section, even when most of that information isn't relevant at the moment they're working on the record. How to decide which organization to use Use conditionals in a single form when there are just a few, related sections. Use multiple forms when the card brings together very different audiences or stages. Split into separate forms information that only makes sense for distinct roles, like requester and approver. Customize color and style for each separate form, for visual identification. Set one of the forms as read-only, if that fits the process. Organization Structure Best for Single form with conditionals One form, fields appear/disappear based on rules A few, related sections Multiple forms on the card Independent side panels, each with its own purpose Very different audiences or stages on the same card Why choose Jestor? Jestor applies the same conditional, permission, and capability rules already used in superforms to multiple forms on a card, so splitting the card into parts doesn't mean losing any customization already available on the platform. Frequently Asked Questions Can each separate form have a different color for visual identification? Yes, you can customize the color and style of each form separately within the same card. Do conditionals work the same way in separate forms as in a single form? Yes, the same conditional rules apply, whether they're in a single form or split across several. Can I set one of the forms as read-only? Yes, you can configure each separate form as editable or read-only. Get to know Jestor at jestor.com and see how to take your company's management to a new level of efficiency and integration.

title: Brookdale Senior Living Earns Certified Most Loved Workplace® Recognition
summary: Brookdale Senior Living announced it has earned Most Loved Workplace® Certification from the Best Practice Institute.
body_text: Brookdale Senior Living Earns Certified Most Loved Workplace® Recognition BRENTWOOD, Tenn., July 23, 2026 – Brookdale Senior Living, the nation’s largest operator of senior living communities and third largest owner of senior living real estate, announced it has earned Most Loved Workplace® Certification from the Best Practice Institute. The certification is awarded to organizations in which employees demonstrate high levels of positive sentiment, aligned values, and an emotional connection to their work, as measured by the Love of Workplace Index® (LOWI) framework. At Brookdale, creating a workplace where associates feel valued is fundamental to delivering quality care for residents. Guided by its mission of enriching the lives of those it serves with compassion, respect, excellence, and integrity, Brookdale believes that when associates feel supported, residents and their families can experience meaningful relationships, an engaging lifestyle, and an increased level of wellness. “Being recognized as a Certified Most Loved Workplace® is a reflection of our associates and the amazing culture we're continually building together,” said Brookdale’s Chief Executive Officer Nick Stengle. “Every day, our teams bring compassion, dedication, and purpose to serving our residents and each other. We are committed to creating an environment where associates feel supported and empowered to do their best work because that is how we deliver more purpose, connection and joy to the families who count on us.” The recognition reflects the company’s focus on workplace culture and associate experience over the past year. Brookdale has worked to strengthen trust, accountability, and associate support across the organization. “This recognition affirms our belief that investing in our people matters,” said Brookdale’s Chief Human Resources Officer Jaclyn Pritchett. “We're focused on listening to our associates, supporting their professional growth, and creating opportunities for them to feel connected to our mission. A strong culture enables us to attract, retain, and develop exceptional associates while delivering quality care for our residents.” Most Loved Workplace® certification is earned following LOWI assessment across the five SPARK dimensions: Systemic Collaboration, Positive Vision of the Future, Alignment of Values, Respect, and Killer Achievement. “What sets Most Loved Workplaces apart is not a score on a survey — it is the depth of emotional connection employees feel to their work, their colleagues, and the future they are building together,” said Louis Carter, CEO and Founder of Best Practice Institute and Most Loved Workplace®. “Brookdale Senior Living demonstrates exactly what the SPARK model reveals in the highest-performing organizations: a positive vision of the future that people believe in, values that are lived not posted, and leaders who create the conditions for people to love where they work. That is not soft. That is a competitive advantage."

title: Coastal States Bank Announces Bill Burrows as Senior Private Banker
summary: Coastal States Bank (“CSB”), a local community bank, announces Bill Burrows as Senior Private Banker
body_text: HILTON HEAD ISLAND, SC (March 3, 2026) – Coastal States Bank (“CSB”) has announced Bill Burrows as Senior Private Banker, based in its Hilton Head Branch at Bow Circle. Serving the bank’s Lowcountry region, Burrows will deliver an integrated banking experience designed to meet the complex needs of individuals, business owners and executives. With more than 15 years of experience spanning commercial, small business and personal banking, he will provide clients with comprehensive strategies and seamless coordination across lending, deposit and treasury solutions. “Bill brings valuable experience and strong local ties to CSB,” said Laura Fraser, CSB’s Lowcountry Market President. “His one-on-one approach and dedication to the Lowcountry reflect our focus on relationship banking, rooted in trust and service for our clients and communities.” Burrows is a native of the Lowcountry and enjoys golf with clients and friends. About the Company Coastal States Bank builds relationships by providing a full range of banking services designed for businesses, their owners and individuals looking for a local banking partner. CSB has a community banking presence in the Lowcountry of South Carolina (Hilton Head Island, Bluffton, Beaufort and Charleston), Savannah and the Atlanta Metropolitan market, and serves communities across the country through its Government Guaranteed Lending, Senior Housing, Correspondent Marine and Mortgage Banker Finance lines of business. At present, CSB has approximately $2.3 billion in total assets. CSB is a wholly-owned subsidiary of CoastalSouth Bancshares, Inc. (NYSE: COSO). Coastal States Bank – Local. And Proud of It.® For additional information regarding Coastal States Bank, please visit www.coastalstatesbank.com . ### Media Contact: Raquel Cobb VP, Marketing and Communications Director Coastal States Bank [email protected]
